Here, beach time can easily be alternated with walks and short trips into the Atlantic Forest. For a relaxed stay, it is better to choose a few favorite beaches than to try to cover the entire coastline.

Itacaré itself offers a more intimate town atmosphere: colorful one- and two-story houses, white churches, cobbled streets, and Afro-Brazilian traditions. On a Bahia itinerary, it makes sense to combine it with Salvador and other stretches of the coast.

Itacuruçá lies on the coast in the Mangaratiba area. Local life revolves around fishing, tourism, and agriculture; small fishermen's houses still stand along the waterfront.

Schooner trips across Sepetiba Bay depart from here. On these outings, visitors see green islands and stop for swimming and walks. Itacuruçá is also included in excursion itineraries departing from Rio de Janeiro.

Itaimbezinho is a canyon in Aparados da Serra National Park in southern Brazil. From the edge of the plateau, almost vertical walls plunge toward the forest-covered floor of the gorge. The canyon's narrow shape makes the contrast between the open grasslands above and the dark depths of the valley especially striking.

Walking trails and viewpoints along the upper rim offer a way to explore the landscape. On clear days, the line of rock walls comes into view, while fog can quickly obscure it. Itaimbezinho is visited from Cambará do Sul, often on a trip combined with Fortaleza Canyon. Available routes and visiting rules should be checked for the specific date.

Itaipu is closely connected with hydroelectric power generation in Paraguay and Brazil. The dam holds back the water and creates a difference in height that drives the turbines. A visit to the complex reveals how a river system can be transformed into a source of electricity.

The structures include a concrete section, a spillway, and areas associated with the reservoir. The size of the dam and the design of its engineering elements are especially impressive when viewed up close. Itaipu adds a distinctive technical attraction to cultural and nature-focused trips through Paraguay, one closely tied to the river and cooperation between the neighboring countries.

The Iximché archaeological complex lies near Tecpán in Guatemala. It was once the capital of the Kaqchikel Maya. The site offers an introduction to the history of a people whose traditions continue in the region, as well as evidence of Maya urban life beyond the best-known sites of Petén.

In 1524, Pedro de Alvarado established the first Spanish capital of Guatemala here. Iximché is therefore associated with two periods of history: the Kaqchikel state and the beginning of the Spanish presence. The complex is visited on the road between Antigua and Lake Atitlán, combining natural scenery with an introduction to the country's early history.
